Quirklessness.text: About one in five people have no Quirk, and the share is smaller among the young. Doctors can usually confirm it in early childhood with an X-ray of the foot: a little toe with a single joint is the common modern pattern and goes with a Quirk, while two joints is the older human pattern and almost always means no Quirk will ever appear. Families often take the diagnosis hard, because hero culture shapes childhood. A Quirkless child is pitied by adults and often teased or bullied by other children, and one who still wants to be a hero is usually told to give up the idea. No law bars Quirkless people from any job, school or exam, and most live ordinary lives as office workers, teachers, doctors, engineers, police officers and parents. Many grandparents are Quirkless and think nothing of it. The barriers are quieter: a teacher's lowered expectations, a sports club that assumes a power, a careless joke at a party, a job interview that drifts toward what the applicant cannot do. Hero work is the one field where the gap is real, since a professional hero has to face people with dangerous Quirks, and no Quirkless hero holds a high ranking. Quirkless adults who choose rescue, police or support work rely on training, gear and judgment, and they earn respect slowly.
